case.label: A
case.text: The strongest case is that the role is described as being for reading reports, so a candidate who reads 'access denied' quickly may think of missing S3 permissions; but the failing call is AssumeRole itself, which the permissions policy does not govern, so only the trust policy change fixes it. The stem does not say what the trust policy holds today, but no other option can make AssumeRole succeed, so no second answer is defensible.

case.label: C
case.text: The stem mentions the private certificate authority, and IAM Roles Anywhere would also deliver temporary credentials without stored keys, even on EC2. But the application already runs on EC2, where an instance profile is the native, lower-overhead path; Roles Anywhere adds trust anchors, profiles and certificate handling. Moving to new instances is also unnecessary because a role can be attached to existing instances. The certificate authority sentence is a deliberate lure, not a second answer.

case.label: B
case.text: IAM users in one central account that switch into roles in each member account is a classic multi-account pattern and does give one sign-in point. But it means managing 300 long-term IAM users plus roles in 40 accounts, and role switching is one account at a time, so it loses on central management and operational overhead against IAM Identity Center with its own identity store.

case.label: C
case.text: The identity pool option that allows all S3 actions meets every functional requirement (temporary credentials, no long-term keys, scales) and only loses on the MOST securely qualifier through least privilege. That makes the decision clear, but the two nearly identical identity pool options form a visible pair that cues the key to one of them; GetFederationToken needs long-term IAM user credentials in the app and Identity Center is for workforce users, so neither is defensible.

case.label: D
case.text: Moving the application to EC2 instances with an instance profile also removes stored long-term credentials and is the standard AWS answer for credentials. But the servers are in the company's data center, so a migration is far more work than IAM Roles Anywhere with the certificate authority the company already runs; the instance profile option without a move cannot work outside EC2 at all.

case.label: C
case.text: A new key with the default key policy would make the existing IAM policy effective, so reads would work afterwards; it is a real fix. But it requires re-encrypting every object and retiring a key, which is far more overhead than one key policy statement. A bucket policy cannot grant KMS permissions, and AdministratorAccess does not help while the key policy does not enable IAM policies, so neither of those is defensible.

case.label: A
case.text: Reading CloudTrail by hand produces the same action list and is fully under the team's control, so it meets the least-privilege requirement. It loses only on overhead against Access Analyzer policy generation, which reads the same trail activity automatically; two months of activity is within the generation window. The credential report does not record actions used by a role, and the policy simulator tests a policy rather than observing use.

case.label: A
case.text: Turning on MFA for the root user is itself a best practice, so a hurried candidate may stop at the first half of this option. But it keeps the root access key and daily root use, which contradict the auditor's request. Permissions boundaries cannot be set on the root user. The key is the only option that both adds MFA and removes the access key, and it is also the most complete-sounding option, which is a mild length cue.

case.label: B
case.text: A candidate could confuse host patching with customer patching duties on services such as EC2, where the customer patches the guest OS. But S3 and DynamoDB are managed services, so host and platform patching and physical security belong to AWS. The key is the only option that mentions IAM permissions, which makes it easy to spot, but no second answer is defensible.

answers.flag: A careful candidate could argue that AD Connector is itself a directory in AWS Directory Service (it has a directory ID and is listed as a directory type), so the constraint 'does not want to run a second directory in AWS' could be read to exclude it and push toward the AD FS SAML federation option, which also needs no password copies; consider rewording the constraint as 'does not want to copy or synchronize the users or passwords into AWS'.

case.label: C
case.text: SAML 2.0 federation from AD FS to an IAM identity provider and roles in each account uses the existing Active Directory credentials, keeps no passwords in AWS and runs no AWS-side directory, so it meets every stated constraint; it loses only on overhead because it needs an identity provider and roles in each of 40 accounts and an AD FS server the stem does not say exists. If a reader treats AD Connector as a second directory in AWS, this option becomes the only one left that meets the constraints.

case.label: C
case.text: A role that allows s3:DeleteObject and requires MFA in its trust policy, with delete removed from the users, also enforces MFA before every delete, and the CLI can assume such a role with an MFA serial in the profile; together with the GetSessionToken step it forms a working combination. It loses on operational overhead because it adds a new role and a policy change, while the condition key change needs one policy edit. S3 MFA Delete covers only version deletion and versioning changes and is enabled by the root user, so it does not meet the rule.

case.label: B
case.text: A company-chosen external ID still adds a condition to the trust policy, so a candidate could see it as equivalent to the vendor-generated ID. But the same value given to every vendor, and not unique per vendor customer, does not stop the confused deputy problem the stem describes. The stem's sentence about a unique ID per customer strongly cues the external ID option, which is the tested point rather than a defect.

case.label: A
case.text: IAM roles are global resources, so one analyzer in one Region does report roles shared outside the organization, and one analyzer has lower overhead. But S3 buckets and KMS keys are regional, and an analyzer reports only the regional resources of its own Region, so buckets and keys in the other two Regions would be missed. The stem's mention of three Regions cues the answer, which is the tested point. Neither option says the analyzer is created in the management account or a delegated administrator account, but that applies to both equally.

case.label: A
case.text: A bucket policy is a valid way to grant S3 read access, so a candidate could pick it. But after AssumeRole the request is made by the role session in the production account, not by the development account, so a bucket policy naming the development account does not match the caller. The stem does not state the role's current permissions policy, but no other option addresses the read failure, so the role permissions change is the only defensible fix.
